But First Nations leaders oppose any changes to or repeal of DRIPA, arguing it provides a reliable framework for government-to-government relations. Canada’s Supreme Court is scheduled to rule Friday, Nov. 27, on Quebec’s Bill 21, which bars some public-sector workers in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols such as hijabs, turbans and kippahs. The justices are also considering whether provinces face limits on using the Charter’s notwithstanding clause to shield laws from rights challenges, and whether courts may still formally declare that a shielded law violates the Charter. Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta have also used the clause, including to protect laws affecting transgender people. Teachers, religious and civil-liberties groups, and the English Montreal School Board challenged Bill 21; lower courts upheld most of the law. The court heard four days of arguments in March and is scheduled to hear a separate Saskatchewan challenge over school pronouns and names in March.

items.title: [news.rthk.hk] Germany warns of AI attack frameworks after EU systems disabled
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) has warned that agentic offensive frameworks (AOFs), including the Artex tool, have reached a high level of maturity. In attacks reported in August and September, AI agents took instructions from human operators, then repeatedly planned, executed and adapted operations. One campaign disabled internal administrative platforms at the European Commission, while another framework was used against hundreds of online shops. The Hong Kong Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) says AI tools let hackers scan systems continuously and find exploitable gaps faster. In a separate study, cybersecurity testing providers reported growing AI use but said humans still oversee high-risk testing: none of the 11 regulated providers surveyed allowed AI to execute tests autonomously. Germany’s BSI and security experts urged organizations to strengthen basic defenses, including incident response, access controls and network separation.

items.title: [phys.org] Neolithic tomb pots point to fermented milk offerings in Denmark
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Researchers studying 330 Neolithic pots from western Zealand, Denmark, found corrosion on 31; 29 came from passage tombs. In experiments with reconstructed vessels, fresh, unpasteurized milk produced damage resembling the marks on ancient pottery, while beer and mead did not. The findings, published in Antiquity, suggest fermented dairy may have been placed with the dead, although corrosion alone cannot identify the contents with certainty. The results challenge an earlier interpretation that the corroded pots held beer, an idea based partly on evidence from brewing communities elsewhere. Fermentation makes milk more acidic, and the researchers say fermented dairy products could also have been easier to digest and lasted longer. Lead author Lone Claudi-Hansen, an archaeologist, said she hopes to examine pottery from other parts of Denmark to see whether the same pattern appears elsewhere.

Researchers analyzing four fossil teeth from two caves in China’s Guangxi region identified Denisovan-related remains and evidence of a potentially distinct ancient human lineage, according to a study published in Nature on Nov. 25. The two Longchuandong teeth align with Denisovans, while two teeth from Chuanshandong—at least 100,800 years old—have traits that do not readily match any known East Asian Homo group. The findings suggest different archaic human populations lived in southern China during overlapping periods, but researchers cannot yet confidently assign the Chuanshandong teeth to a named group. Warm, humid conditions in the region hinder ancient DNA preservation, so researchers analyzed tooth shape and proteins. They say more fossils and molecular evidence are needed to establish the teeth’s evolutionary relationships.

A permanent director must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, which Democrats are due to control in January. Cybersecurity experts say companies’ rapid efforts to patch software vulnerabilities may be behind some disruptions, as advanced AI tools make those flaws easier to find.

items.title: [grist.org] El Niño-linked downpours flood Southwest and Florida, killing at least four
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Intense storms caused severe flooding in the U.S. Southwest and Florida in late October and early November, killing at least four people in the Southwest. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook favors wetter conditions across much of the southern United States through February 2027 as a strong El Niño develops. Warm Pacific waters can increase atmospheric moisture, while recent rain left rivers high and soils saturated in parts of the Southwest, worsening runoff when further storms arrived. The winter’s snowpack remains uncertain; Colorado climatologist Russ Schumacher said rainfall could help the Colorado River’s reservoirs but would not reverse their decline.

items.title: [thestar.com] Doctors warn Wainwright fire injuries may require years of recovery
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Nearly six weeks after a wind-driven grass fire burned soldiers during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, doctors say some face months or years of physical and psychological recovery. Five soldiers have died; as of Thursday, 19 injured soldiers remained in Alberta hospitals, seven in critical condition, while the military said 22 were still hospitalized across Canada. Burn specialist Dr. Josh Wong said treatment for severe burns can involve repeated surgeries, rehabilitation and ongoing psychological support. The fire overwhelmed the Edmonton burn unit, and three investigations are examining how it started and why live-fire training continued as strong winds pushed flames across the base. Health officials say they will review the emergency response after addressing immediate treatment needs.

items.title: [stirileprotv.ro] Researchers identify possible largest known scorpion, over one meter long
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Researchers have identified Praearcturus gigas, a scorpion known from a fossil found in the United Kingdom dating to about 415 million years ago, as a candidate for the largest known scorpion. They estimated that the animal exceeded one meter in length. A new analysis combining CT scans with traditional fossil tracings resolved decades of uncertainty over its classification. Paleontologist Richie Howard and colleagues infer that it hunted both on land and in water; terrestrial ecosystems were still developing at the time. The researchers suggest that the absence of other large predators may have enabled its large size, while later competition may have contributed to its decline.

items.title: [theguardian.com] Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted Riemann claim prompts math departments to adapt
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says the company’s Claude assistant helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis, a longstanding mathematical claim about prime-number distribution. The claimed proof remains subject to human verification. Johns Hopkins University’s mathematics department has issued guidance for Ph.D. applicants and job candidates, saying it expects transparency about AI use and will not give written work positive weight unless candidates demonstrate they understand it. Professor Yiannis Sakellaridis said the guidance was prompted by the risk that candidates could submit AI-generated proofs without learning the underlying mathematics, not by a specific applicant case. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei rejected the idea that people should hand governance to AI, while David Krueger, founder of the nonprofit Evitable, argued that concern about losing control calls for a halt to advanced AI development. Researchers and technology leaders have debated whether the mathematical advances signal progress toward systems that exceed human capabilities.
